summary:
On long missions, astronauts have to notice changes in their own health, and the farther they are from Earth, the longer help takes to arrive. A message to Mars can take up to 22 minutes each way, and deep space can mean hours or a total blackout. NoTime2Die is a health copilot that knows how far Earth is.

It gathers health indicators like heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen, sleep, radiation dose, mood, symptoms and reaction time from a daily check in and a short vigilance test. A risk engine scores each body system as green, amber or red. Every alert explains why it fired and links the NASA source behind its threshold, so astronauts can trust it instead of guessing.

What makes it different is the comms delay setting. Near Earth, an alert loops in the flight surgeon. On Mars, the same alert turns into step by step actions the crew can do right away, with a summary sent home. In deep space or during a blackout, the crew gets the full protocol and Earth gets a log later. A live body map, a mission timeline with real NASA DONKI solar particle events, and a scripted demo mode tie it all together.

The astronaut owns their data, everything stays on the device unless they choose to share it, and there's no surveillance score. It's a research prototype, not a medical device. The idea and design decisions came from our team, and we used Cursor as an AI coding assistant to help build it.
details:
What it does and how it works
NoTime2Die is a health monitoring copilot for astronauts on long missions, and it knows how far Earth is. It gathers health indicators like heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, breathing rate, skin temperature, sleep, exercise, cumulative radiation dose, mood, symptoms and reaction time. Some come from a simulated wearable stream, others from a 90 second daily check in and a short vigilance test. A risk engine checks each body system (heart, radiation, bone and muscle, sleep and fatigue, behavioral health, vision, immune) and marks it green, amber or red. Every alert explains why it fired and links the NASA source behind its threshold. A comms delay setting goes from ISS to Moon, Mars and deep space, plus a blackout mode, and it changes what the app tells the crew. Near Earth, an alert loops in the flight surgeon. On Mars, the crew gets step by step actions to do right away, while a summary goes home. In deep space or during a blackout, the crew runs the full protocol alone and Earth gets a log later.

Benefits
Astronauts can spot problems early and understand them, because no alert is a black box. They know exactly what to do even when Earth can't answer in time. Everything is in one screen: a live body map, trends over the mission, and clear next steps.

Intended impact
Missions to Mars and beyond will have long comms delays and blackouts, so crews won't always have a doctor on call. NoTime2Die is built for that shift toward Earth independent medical care, where the crew leads and Earth acts as a consultant. The same idea could also help remote places on Earth, like polar stations, ships or rural clinics.

Tools, languages and software
Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, Recharts, Zustand and Vitest, all running in the browser with no backend. We used NASA's DONKI space weather data for real solar particle events, plus NASA Human Research Program sources for the radiation, bone loss, sleep and comms delay figures. Cursor helped us write the code as an AI coding assistant. No special hardware is needed, and the data is simulated because real astronaut health records are private.

How it's creative
Most health dashboards act the same everywhere. Ours changes how much it hands to the crew as Earth gets farther away. In the demo, one radiation alert flips live from "contact Earth" to "here's what to do now" to full autonomy just by sliding the delay. It also feels like a real mission control screen, with a body map that pulses where the risk is.

Factors our team considered
Privacy and trust came first. The astronaut owns their data, it stays on the device unless they choose to share it, and there's no surveillance score. Every number is sourced, or clearly labeled as a demo assumption. Alerts never rely on color alone. We kept it cheap by using sensors crews already wear, like Astroskin, instead of new hardware. It's a research prototype, not a medical device. The idea and design came from our team, and AI was only used to help write code.
